title: How a water-quality problem becomes a planning bar
paras: Let's start with how a water-quality problem becomes a planning bar. Nutrient neutrality isn't a policy an authority can weigh and set aside — it's the hard consequence of a legal duty, and it can't be balanced away. It comes from the Habitats Regulations, which brought the European habitats and birds directives into our law. Brexit didn't change that: they still bind as assimilated law, and the European case law reading them still carries weight, subject to the higher courts' power to depart from it. The regulation numbers, statutory instruments and case citations all live in the written guide, so I'll stay on the ideas.

The mechanism: where a plan or project is likely to have a significant effect on a European site — a special area of conservation or protection area — alone or in combination with everything else, and it isn't about managing the site itself, the competent authority must carry out an appropriate assessment against the site's conservation objectives. For an ordinary application that's the local planning authority; on appeal or call-in, the Secretary of State or an inspector. The trigger is deliberately low and precautionary — a real risk you can't rule out is enough. Then the standard: the authority can only agree once satisfied the scheme won't harm the site's integrity. Not a balancing exercise, and benefits outweighing harm won't do — it's a threshold, met only if it's sure, to no reasonable scientific doubt, that integrity won't be harmed. So where new homes or overnight accommodation add load to a site already in unfavourable condition from enrichment, it can't reach that certainty unless the extra load is cancelled out. That's neutrality — the applicant shows the development is neutral, so the authority can lawfully find no adverse effect.

Two features to hold. It's a two-stage filter — screen for likely significant effects, then a full assessment if you can't rule them out. But since People Over Wind you can't screen a real nutrient risk out by pointing to mitigation, so in an affected catchment the full assessment is unavoidable for anything with overnight population. And though the authority owns the conclusion, it must consult Natural England, whose advice carries very substantial weight — it can in principle depart with cogent reasons and its own evidence, but almost never does, because the integrity test demands certainty and that advice is the safest route to it. So the advice, though only guidance, works almost as if binding.

There is a way past the integrity test, but few schemes can use it. A project can proceed despite a negative assessment where there are imperative reasons of overriding public interest, no alternative solutions, and secured compensatory measures protecting the coherence of the national site network. For nationally significant infrastructure or major strategic development you can occasionally run it — narrower still where the site holds a priority habitat or species, and there you may even need a European Commission-style opinion before it's entertained. But for housing, a holiday-let conversion or a modest rural scheme it's a dead end: the 'no alternative solutions' limb alone usually defeats it, since a differently sited or mitigated scheme is nearly always available. Neutrality, not the derogation, is the answer.

title: The case law that set the approach
paras: Now the case law. The regime bites this hard because of a handful of decisions. First, from the European court in 2018, People Over Wind: mitigation cannot be taken into account at the screening stage. You can't note a proposal comes with measures to cut its nutrient impact and screen it out on that basis — the mitigation has to be tested inside the full assessment, under the precautionary standard. So that exercise is engaged wherever a real nutrient risk exists, with the applicant carrying the burden. Before it, authorities screened these effects out; after it, they can't.

The companion Dutch Nitrogen rulings struck down a programmatic approach to nitrogen because it leaned on the future benefits of measures whose effectiveness wasn't yet established. The lesson carried across: you can't discharge the integrity test by pointing to future or uncertain improvements — the benefit has to be real, secured and effective before it counts, which is why neutrality mitigation must be locked in perpetuity and demonstrably additional. Domestically the methodology survived Wyatt, where the Court of Appeal rejected a challenge to Natural England's precautionary budget approach: building in conservative assumptions and erring on the side of the site isn't irrational, it's what the directive requires. That's your answer to the client who says the assumptions are too cautious.

The big recent one is C G Fry, in the Supreme Court. The assessment duty can be engaged not just at outline permission but at the later reserved-matters or discharge-of-conditions stage, where that approval is what lets the project proceed — even where the outline predated Natural England's nutrient advice. An old permission is no safe harbour: if details still need approving, the assessment can catch the scheme on the way through. The company still won, but narrowly — its site, the Somerset Levels and Moors, is a Ramsar site, protected in England through Government policy, not the Habitats Regulations as statute, so the strict duty didn't bite as argued. That gap is narrow and closing: the 2025 Planning and Infrastructure Act puts Ramsar sites on the same statutory footing as European sites, so don't build a strategy on it — and check the commencement of that provision before relying on it.

One more line, Ashdown Forest and Wealden: in-combination effects — there, recreational pressure and traffic air pollution — must be assessed, and failing to is unlawful. Neutrality is an in-combination problem par excellence: one house adds little, but every house adds to a load the site can't absorb. That's why it's assessed cumulatively, and why 'my scheme is tiny' is no answer.

title: The science, for planners
paras: Now the science, briefly — you need the mechanism, because the mitigation follows from it. These protected sites are freshwater and estuarine habitats that depend on low nutrient levels. Too much nitrogen or phosphorus and the water enriches, algae and plant growth explode, and as it decays it strips out the oxygen — eutrophication. Algal blooms, choked deoxygenated water, protected species and habitats in decline. Because the site is already at or beyond its limit, the law won't tolerate any net addition without compensation.

The two nutrients differ, and which drives a catchment shapes the budget. Phosphorus usually limits rivers, so many affected river sites are phosphate-led — the Wye and Lugg, the Somerset Levels and Moors, the Axe. Nitrogen limits coastal and estuarine waters, so those are nitrate-led — the Solent above all, and Stodmarsh in Kent. Some count both. A Wye budget counts kilograms of phosphorus a year, a Solent budget kilograms of nitrogen, and the mitigation has to be in the same currency as the harm.

The nutrients come from two places: wastewater from the population a development adds, and agricultural run-off. Planning can't touch the farming, which is usually the larger source, but it can control the one thing new development undeniably adds — overnight population, whose sewage, even treated, still carries nutrients into the catchment. That's why the trigger is people sleeping on the site. Add no overnight population and you add no new load of this kind, and generally no problem. Everything about what's caught flows from that.

title: What actually triggers a requirement
paras: So what triggers a requirement? The question is blunt: does the proposal put more people sleeping in the catchment than before? If it does, and the site drains to an affected protected site, neutrality is in play. The clearest case is net additional dwellings — any scale, from a strategic urban extension to a single open-market house or an annexe that becomes an independent dwelling. Numbers don't save you: one dwelling in the Solent needs a budget and mitigation just as a hundred do, because the duty operates cumulatively.

Beyond housing, the net catches overnight visitor accommodation in every form, and this is where rural and tourism clients get caught. Holiday lets, glamping pods, cabins, shepherd's huts, touring and static caravan pitches, hotels, bed-and-breakfast — all add overnight population, all must be neutral. A barn to a holiday let, or six glamping pods in a paddock, is exactly what the regime bites on, however modest or green. Residential institutions — care homes, student accommodation, hostels — are caught too, and their occupancy can run higher per unit than housing. And a change of use adding overnight population is caught even with no building work: barn to dwelling, office to flats, a house to a house in multiple occupation with more bedrooms.

What's generally not caught adds no overnight population — most commercial, employment, retail and industrial floorspace; day tourism like a café or farm shop; agricultural buildings in genuine agricultural use; like-for-like replacement that doesn't add bedrooms or units. Watch the grey areas: a materially larger replacement dwelling, or one with more bedrooms, can add occupancy and a marginal load; extensions adding bedrooms can too on some approaches; mixed day-and-overnight schemes need the overnight part isolated. And watch the permitted-development route into residential — barn to dwelling under Class Q, commercial to flats under Class MA. The Habitats duty doesn't switch off because the route is permitted development: prior approval is light-touch, but the integrity duty is an absolute bar where an adverse effect can't be ruled out, and it prevails. So no authority can lawfully grant prior approval for a conversion in an affected catchment unless neutrality is shown — which largely defeats the fast-track, since the applicant still needs a budget and secured mitigation. For a client eyeing Class Q on a barn in the Wye or Somerset catchment, that's unwelcome news to deliver early. Permitted development is not an escape.

And the burden sits squarely on the applicant. The authority owns the assessment but can only conclude 'no adverse effect' if the budget and secured mitigation before it allow — no robust budget and deliverable mitigation, no grant, and the application just stalls. There's no route by which the authority absorbs the problem: the work and cost fall on the applicant, and permission doesn't come until neutrality is demonstrated.

title: The nutrient budget
paras: Now the nutrient budget — the document that decides the case; you should be able to read one critically even if you never build one. It uses Natural England's methodology and catchment calculators, and the logic is a before-and-after of the load leaving the site. On the proposed side, the calculator takes the new overnight population — from the number and size of dwellings, or the accommodation's occupancy, on standard assumptions — applies an assumed per-person water use and the nutrient concentration of the treated wastewater serving the site, then adds any change in export from the land use itself, because a field taken out of arable and built on, or a paddock turned to garden, changes what runs off. On the existing side it credits the land's current lawful use. The adjusted difference is the net load, in kilograms of nitrogen or phosphorus a year.

Two things matter when you sense-check a figure. It's deliberately precautionary — a buffer, commonly around twenty per cent, and conservative assumptions throughout, because Wyatt confirms erring on the side of the site is what the law requires; a client who says the numbers are pessimistic is right, and beside the point. And the land-use component swings the result more than people expect: a development on intensively farmed land can, on paper, reduce the load against the farming baseline, while one on low-nutrient land like permanent pasture starts lower and shows a larger net addition — counter-intuitive, and where budgets get argued over. You want a net figure that's zero or negative after mitigation — neutral or better. A positive residual means it isn't neutral and can't be permitted until it is.

And the punchline: for a single dwelling the net figure might be only a few kilograms of nitrogen a year — yet securing even that, in perpetuity, through additional and monitored land management, is neither cheap nor always possible. That's the difficulty in a sentence.

title: Mitigation — the routes and their catches
paras: Now mitigation. Four broad ways to close a budget, each with a catch. First, on-site: where the site can take it, remove the load on land you control — wetlands or reedbeds that strip nutrients, land out of intensive agriculture, sustainable drainage that cuts export. On a large site with spare land that works, secured through the permission. On a small site it usually can't — a single dwelling or a few glamping pods rarely has the land for a meaningful, monitorable, permanent reduction, and a token pond won't satisfy the precautionary standard. So most modest schemes are pushed towards buying credits.

Second, off-site credits — securing reduction elsewhere in the same catchment and tying it to the permission. Two sources: Natural England's own mitigation scheme, launched in 2023, selling credits from habitat schemes it has funded; and a private market of habitat banks selling directly. Either way the mitigation must be additional — it wouldn't have happened anyway — secured in perpetuity, in practice the development's lifetime, commonly eighty to a hundred and twenty-five years, and guaranteed and monitored, because Dutch Nitrogen won't let an authority count an uncertain future benefit. The mechanics usually run through a section 106 or a conservation covenant, tying credits to the permission and blocking occupation until the mitigation is in place. The catches are price and availability: credits are expensive, the price per kilogram volatile, and in some catchments at some times there are none to buy — and then the scheme can't proceed, however willing the applicant. That's a real viability problem, and it belongs in the advice from day one.

Third, land-use change — the flip side, and an opportunity for landowners. Taking land out of intensive production — arable or intensive grassland to low-input grassland, woodland or wetland — cuts the load, and that reduction can be sold as mitigation. For a farm under pressure, a well-placed block can be worth more as offset than as marginal production. To be credible it needs exactly what the case law demands: genuine and additional — not what the land would have done anyway, not double-counted against another subsidy — quantified on Natural England's methodology, secured in perpetuity, and monitored. A vague promise to farm less intensively won't do; a mapped, quantified, legally secured reduction will. For rural clients this is one of the few genuinely positive angles.

Fourth, strategic solutions — because the largest source in most catchments is existing wastewater and farming, not new housing. There's now a statutory duty on water companies to upgrade the designated significant treatment works — broadly those serving two thousand people or more — to a demanding nutrient-removal standard by 2030. Where a development drains to such works, the authority must assume the upgrade will be delivered by the deadline, which lowers the assumed load and can improve a budget. The catch is timing: it helps the baseline in 2030, not the applicant building now, and doesn't by itself make a present scheme neutral. It shifts the arithmetic at the margin, not the need for mitigation today.

The intended strategic answer is the Nature Restoration Fund and environmental delivery plans under the 2025 Act. Rather than each developer chasing scarce credits, they pay a levy into the Fund, Natural England discharges the obligation strategically through a delivery plan approved by the Secretary of State, and the duty is treated as met. If it works, the credit-scarcity bottleneck goes. But as things stand in mid-2026 it isn't available: the Act is in force, the enabling regulations were laid before Parliament in June, and Natural England is about to consult on the first draft plan for nutrients — but a plan must be consulted on, at least twenty-eight days, then approved, before it can be relied on, and none is operational. An applicant needing a decision this year can't use it and still needs a conventional budget and secured mitigation. Treat the Fund as the direction of travel, not a present option, and don't let a client defer a live application on it.

title: The consultant’s playbook
paras: So, the playbook. First, triage: is the site within, or does it drain to, a catchment covered by Natural England's nutrient advice, and does the proposal add overnight population? Natural England publishes the mapping and affected authorities keep it on their websites; a site outside every catchment, or with no overnight use, is clear. If it's caught, scope it before design is fixed, because mitigation availability and cost may decide whether the scheme is viable at all — far cheaper at inception than after a year of design. PlanRef's constraints map carries the catchment layer, so check there first.

Be honest about time and cost. Neutrality routinely adds months and a material sum, and on small schemes the mitigation cost can be a decisive share of value — enough to sink a marginal barn conversion or a two-plot infill. Where a scheme leans on credits, deliverability turns on a market that has, at times and places, had nothing to sell, so don't let a client exchange contracts assuming credits will be there. And where the scheme is phased, remember C G Fry — a later approval can itself trigger the assessment, so an old outline is no shield, and mitigation needs planning across the whole build-out.

It interacts directly with housing delivery. In the worst-hit areas — the Solent above all — neutrality stalled tens of thousands of homes for years and blew holes in five-year land supply, which then engages the tilted balance and the wider decision-making arithmetic we cover elsewhere. The bar suppresses delivery, that weakens supply, and weakened supply changes how other applications across the district get decided.

For rural and tourism clients especially — farm diversification, holiday lets, a barn to overnight use — raise neutrality before the client falls in love with the scheme, because it's exactly these modest, land-based proposals that are caught, struggle to mitigate on-site, and can be tipped into unviability by credit costs. The corollary: a farmer with the wrong land for a holiday let may have the right land to sell as offset. The recurring mistakes are all here — thinking a small or green scheme is too minor or exempt, that permitted development sidesteps the duty, that the Fund can be relied on now, or leaving the question to validation when it should have shaped the scheme from the start.

title: Boundaries and related regimes
paras: Two boundary points keep English practitioners out of trouble. First, Wales. Neutrality is a UK-wide consequence of the Habitats Regulations, but the detail differs across the border: the adviser is Natural Resources Wales, which set phosphorus targets for the Welsh river sites, with its own framework and mitigation arrangements. It shows most on the River Wye, whose catchment straddles Powys and Herefordshire — one river system, two regulators, two regimes. And the 2025 Act, the Nature Restoration Fund and the water-company upgrade duty are English measures that don't apply in Wales. Don't read across.

Second, neutrality is only one of the effects the Habitats Regulations require to be assessed. The same duty catches recreational pressure — why coastal and heathland authorities require alternative greenspace and contributions for housing near the New Forest, Thames Basin Heaths or Dorset heaths — and traffic air quality, the Ashdown Forest issue. Separate assessments, separate mitigation, and a site can be caught by more than one. And keep it distinct from ordinary drainage control: plenty of development is conditioned for foul and surface-water drainage, phosphate-stripping treatment plants or a mains connection — sensible, but not neutrality, and they don't discharge the Habitats duty. Neutrality is the specific requirement, driven by a European-site designation and the integrity test, to show a net-neutral nutrient effect through secured, additional, perpetual mitigation. No affected European site and you're in the ordinary drainage world; where there is one, a drainage condition alone won't save the application.

title: The road ahead
paras: Finally, the road ahead. The Government has tried more than once to remove neutrality and hasn't. In 2023 it proposed to disapply the requirement for housing, through amendments to what became the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act, and the House of Lords threw them out later that year. The requirement stood. That's often misremembered: the duty was not removed, and anyone who tells a client otherwise is wrong.

The strategy now isn't to abolish the duty but to discharge it strategically — the water-company upgrades improving the baseline by 2030, and the Nature Restoration Fund and delivery plans that would pool the mitigation instead of each developer chasing scarce credits. If those land, the burden on applicants should ease, and the C G Fry Ramsar gap will by then be closed by the 2025 Act. But none of it is operational yet. So advise on the law and market as they are, treat the reforms as prospects to track, not tools to use, and revisit the moment the first plan is made — because in this subject, more than any other, last year's note is a liability.
